headline: AMD Makes Record Profits from AI Computers, But Gaming Gear Gets Pricier

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: AMD is a company that makes computer chips, which are tiny parts that help computers think and work. AMD just had its best three months ever, earning more money than at any other time in its history. Most of this money came from selling chips used in "data centers." Data centers are huge buildings full of powerful computers that help run things like artificial intelligence, or AI, which is computer software that can learn and make decisions almost like a person. Because so many companies want AI, AMD is selling tons of chips for these giant computer buildings. But there is a downside. Because factories are making so many parts for AI computers, there aren't enough parts left over for things like video game consoles and gaming computers. This has made gaming computers and consoles more expensive. AMD's gaming business actually made less money this year because of this. Experts think this shortage of parts might not get better for several years, meaning gamers might keep paying higher prices for a while.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: AMD, a major computer chip company, just announced its most successful and profitable quarter ever. The company earned $13.4 billion in just three months, and it expects to earn even more next quarter — around $17 billion. Most of this huge growth is coming from AMD's data center business, which makes chips for the giant computer systems that power artificial intelligence (AI). Data centers now make up 63% of AMD's total earnings, and the company predicts that number could grow to over 80% by 2027. While AMD's AI-related business is booming, its gaming division is struggling. Sales of gaming chips dropped 40% compared to last year. This is partly because of a shortage of computer memory parts, called RAM, which are needed to build gaming computers, consoles, and other everyday electronics. Since AI data centers need so much memory, there isn't enough RAM left for companies that make consumer products like laptops and gaming systems. This shortage is pushing prices up for regular shoppers. Other tech companies, like Intel and SK Hynix, warn that this shortage could last for years — possibly until 2030. AMD's own CEO admitted that shoppers are becoming more careful with their money because of rising prices, and the company expects a slower year for its gaming and consumer products in 2027, even as its AI business keeps growing rapidly.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: AMD, a leading computer chip manufacturer, just reported the most profitable quarter in the company's history, earning a record $13.4 billion in just three months. The company expects even bigger results next quarter, predicting $17 billion in revenue. This growth is being driven almost entirely by AMD's data center business — the division that makes powerful chips used to run artificial intelligence (AI) systems in massive server warehouses. Data centers already generate 63% of AMD's total revenue, and the company's financial officer, Jean Hu, said she expects that number to climb above 80% by 2027. In other words, AMD is quickly transforming from a company that sells chips for everyday computers and video games into one that mainly powers AI infrastructure. However, this shift comes with a tradeoff. As factories focus on producing memory chips and parts for AI data centers, there's less supply available for consumer products like gaming PCs, laptops, and video game consoles. This has caused a shortage of RAM (computer memory) and driven up prices on everyday electronics. AMD's own gaming division suffered because of this, with its gaming-related revenue dropping 40% compared to last year, falling to $773 million. Rival chipmakers Intel and SK Hynix both warned that this shortage isn't likely to end soon — Intel doesn't expect improvement in 2027, and SK Hynix predicts the shortage could last until 2030. AMD's CEO, Lisa Su, acknowledged that rising prices are making everyday consumers more cautious about buying new tech, leading to a slowdown in sales. As a result, AMD is preparing for what it calls a "down year" for its gaming and consumer electronics business in 2027, even while its AI-focused data center business continues to set new records. This story reflects a larger trend in the tech industry: as companies race to build AI infrastructure, the resources needed for everyday consumer technology are becoming scarcer and more expensive.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: AMD, one of the world's largest computer chip manufacturers, just posted the most profitable quarter in its history, earning a record-breaking $13.4 billion in a single quarter. The company expects even stronger results ahead, forecasting $17 billion in revenue for the next quarter. This explosive growth is being fueled almost entirely by AMD's data center division, which designs and sells the specialized chips that power the massive server farms running artificial intelligence (AI) systems. During the most recent quarter, data center sales alone brought in $8.5 billion, and the division now accounts for 63% of AMD's total revenue. Looking ahead, AMD's chief financial officer, Jean Hu, said she expects data centers to make up more than 80% of the company's entire business by 2027 — a dramatic shift that shows how central AI has become to the chip industry's bottom line. However, this AI boom has a significant downside for everyday consumers. As chip manufacturers redirect their production toward AI data centers, there's a growing shortage of RAM (random-access memory) and other components needed to build consumer electronics like laptops, desktop computers, and video game consoles. This shortage has already caused price increases across the tech industry, and it's hurting companies' consumer-facing businesses. AMD's own gaming division, for example, saw its revenue plunge 40% compared to last year, falling to just $773 million. Other major chipmakers are warning that the shortage won't resolve quickly. Intel has said it doesn't expect conditions to improve in 2027, while SK Hynix, a major memory chip manufacturer, predicts the shortage could persist until as late as 2030. AMD's CEO, Lisa Su, acknowledged that higher prices are making consumers more cautious, leading to slower sales in markets like gaming. Because of this, AMD says it's bracing for what it calls a "down year" in its consumer-focused business during 2027 — even as its AI-driven data center business continues to break records. This situation highlights a broader economic pattern taking shape across the tech world: as companies pour enormous resources into building AI infrastructure, the supply of parts available for ordinary consumer products shrinks, and prices for everyday electronics — from gaming consoles to laptops — tend to rise as a result.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: AMD, one of the two dominant companies designing computer processors alongside Intel, has reported the most profitable quarter in its corporate history, generating a record $13.4 billion in revenue over three months. The company's momentum shows no sign of slowing: it projects $17 billion in revenue for the upcoming quarter, an increase driven almost entirely by surging demand in its data center division. That segment, which produces specialized chips for the massive server infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence (AI) computing, brought in $8.5 billion last quarter alone and now represents 63% of AMD's total business. CEO Lisa Su projects the company's overall revenue will grow more than 80% in 2027, with data centers remaining the primary engine of that expansion. Even more striking, CFO Jean Hu indicated that by 2027, data center sales could account for more than 80% of AMD's entire revenue — a transformation that would fundamentally redefine what kind of company AMD is, shifting it from a broad-based chipmaker into one whose fortunes are overwhelmingly tied to the AI computing boom. This restructuring of AMD's business reflects a wider trend reshaping the global technology supply chain. As AI companies race to build out server farms capable of training and running advanced AI models, demand for memory chips, processors, and other hardware components has skyrocketed. This has created intense competition for limited manufacturing capacity, and consumer electronics are bearing the cost. AMD's own gaming division, which makes chips for PCs and game consoles, saw its revenue drop 40% year-over-year to $773 million, a casualty of a broader shortage of RAM (computer memory) and related components. This scarcity has already pushed up prices for everyday consumer electronics like laptops, desktop computers, and gaming consoles. The shortage appears likely to persist: Intel has stated it doesn't anticipate relief in 2027, while SK Hynix, a leading memory chip manufacturer, projects the imbalance could last until 2030. Su acknowledged the economic pressure this is placing on ordinary consumers, noting that rising system prices have made buyers more price-sensitive, resulting in a noticeable slowdown in sales. As a result, AMD is explicitly planning for a "down year" in its consumer-oriented business during 2027, even as its AI-driven data center operations continue setting records. This divergence — soaring AI profits alongside a struggling consumer tech market — illustrates a significant economic tension emerging from the AI boom: while corporations investing in AI infrastructure reap enormous financial rewards, ordinary consumers may face years of higher prices and limited availability for everyday technology as global manufacturing capacity gets redirected toward satisfying the AI industry's seemingly insatiable demand for computing power.

questions: If prices for laptops, gaming consoles, or computer parts keep rising because of AI demand, how might that affect what you or your family can afford to buy?
Do you think it's fair that companies are prioritizing AI data centers over everyday consumer products like gaming devices? Why or why not?
How do you think this shift toward AI-focused technology might change the kinds of jobs or skills that will be valuable in the future?
